name: mTCP
workload: Short-lived TCP connection handling / small-message request-response transactions on multicore Linux, plus ported applications (e.g. lighttpd) comparing the user-level mTCP stack to the stock Linux TCP stack.
claimed_speedup: up to 25x faster than the latest Linux TCP stack for small-message transactions; ~3x faster than the best-performing prior user-level TCP research system; 33% to 320% throughput improvement for ported applications
tradeoffs: Requires a dedicated packet-I/O driver (DPDK, PacketShader, or netmap) and cores reserved for the mTCP stack; exposes its own epoll-like API rather than drop-in POSIX sockets, so applications must be ported.
caveats: NSDI 2014 best-paper-winning peer-reviewed paper, but the page/PDF text extracted via WebFetch did not surface the exact CPU model or compiler flags, so tier is capped at B rather than A. The paper names the baseline generically as 'the Linux TCP stack'; epoll is inferred as the specific mechanism being beaten via the ported comparison applications (e.g. lighttpd), not quoted verbatim in the abstract.

name: IX (protected dataplane OS)
workload: memcached key-value store request throughput and tail latency, IX dataplane OS vs stock Linux.
claimed_speedup: up to 3.6x higher memcached throughput and more than 2x lower tail latency vs Linux
tradeoffs: Research prototype OS requiring a custom kernel/dataplane split (built on the Dune hardware-virtualization mechanism); not a drop-in library and not portable to stock Linux without OS-level changes.
caveats: OSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper, but no public source-code repository could be located (checked GitHub), so per the 'papers with no code' rule the tier is capped at C despite peer review. The paper names the baseline generically as 'Linux'; memcached's own event library (libevent, layered over epoll) is inferred as the specific mechanism being beaten rather than quoted verbatim.

name: Arrakis
baseline: epoll (well-tuned Linux network stack, Redis-like persistent NoSQL store)
workload: Persistent NoSQL key-value store (Redis-like) request latency and throughput, Arrakis split-kernel OS vs a well-tuned Linux implementation.
claimed_speedup: 2-5x lower latency and up to 9x higher throughput vs a well-tuned Linux implementation
tradeoffs: Requires a custom split-kernel OS (Barrelfish-derived) and virtualized/SR-IOV-capable NIC hardware; not portable to stock Linux; no public source release found.
caveats: OSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper, but no public code repository was found (checked GitHub), so per the 'papers with no code' rule the tier is capped at C despite peer review. 'Well-tuned Linux implementation' is the paper's own wording; epoll usage by the comparison Redis-like store is inferred, not quoted verbatim in the retrieved abstract/summary.

name: io_uring hybrid storage I/O architecture (Oracle Database)
workload: TPC-C (OLTP) and TPC-H (analytical) database I/O workloads, plus an isolated write-path microbenchmark, comparing io_uring-based storage I/O to the prior libaio-based path in Oracle Database at production scale.
claimed_speedup: OLTP (TPC-C): identical throughput with server CPU utilization reduced by 1.2 percentage points; TPC-H: CPU per query drops 8.5% (geomean); isolated write-path: 29% lower CPU per write and 34% higher throughput; synchronous reads at very large I/O sizes show no improvement or a regression
tradeoffs: Findings are architecture/design guidance embedded in a proprietary closed-source RDBMS, not a reusable open library; benefit is workload-dependent and regresses for very large synchronous reads.
caveats: First-party benchmark by Oracle Database engineers evaluating their own closed-source product; hardware and compiler/build details were not surfaced on the arXiv abstract page; the paper references artifacts at a Zenodo DOI, but the database source itself is not public.
